title: Why Is the Dollar Green?

fin.small: Sources: Bank of Canada Museum (2019); U.S. Currency Education Program, History; U.S. BEP, Currency FAQs

parts: The ink that may explain the green dollar was invented in Canada.
In eighteen fifty-seven, a chemist in Quebec, Thomas Sterry Hunt, got a request.
The president of a Montreal bank wanted an ink to stop forgers.
Hunt made a green tint from chromium oxide.
It was called Canada Bank Note Tint.
That summer, the bankers' group against forgery did not recommend it.
Other chemists found ways to remove it.
Four years later, U.S. printers used green anyway.
The new notes had green backs. People called them greenbacks.
The U.S. Bureau of Engraving later wrote that green ink was believed to beat forgers with cameras.
But it also says no definite explanation can be made for the original choice.
Our reading: the best clue to America's green is a Canadian lab.
